# Numerical Investigation of Barrett-Crane Models in Riemannian Quantum Gravity

## Introduction and Motivation

This study presents a numerical investigation of Barrett-Crane models of Riemannian quantum gravity, aiming to develop a deeper and more quantitative understanding of their dynamical behavior. While the Barrett-Crane model has been extensively studied from an analytical and formal perspective as a spin foam approach to quantum gravity, numerical methods offer a complementary avenue for probing its physical content, particularly in regimes where analytical techniques become intractable. By computing explicit numerical results, this work seeks to illuminate features of the model that might otherwise remain hidden in purely formal treatments.

## Methodological Extensions

A central contribution of this work is the extension of existing numerical techniques to accommodate the q-deformed version of the Barrett-Crane model. The q-deformation, which introduces a quantum group structure parameterized by q, is of particular interest because it is expected to implement a cosmological constant in the theory and to render the state sum finite. Adapting the numerical machinery to handle these q-deformed models required careful modification of the algorithms used to evaluate the relevant spin network amplitudes and vertex weights, thereby broadening the scope of phenomena that can be explored numerically within this framework.

In addition to incorporating q-deformation, the researchers generalized their computational techniques to handle arbitrary space-time triangulations, rather than restricting the analysis to simple or highly symmetric simplicial complexes. This generalization significantly increases the flexibility and applicability of the numerical approach, allowing the model to be studied on a wider variety of discretized manifolds and enabling more robust tests of whether observed features are artifacts of a particular triangulation or genuine properties of the underlying continuum physics.

## Computation and Interpretation of Observables

With these extended techniques in hand, the researchers computed expectation values for a selection of physically motivated observables. Among these, particular attention was given to a spin-spin correlation function, which serves as a probe of the correlations between geometric degrees of freedom at different locations within the triangulated spacetime. The behavior of this and other observables was analyzed in order to extract qualitative and quantitative insights into how the Barrett-Crane model behaves under various conditions, including different triangulations and values of the deformation parameter q. This analysis provides valuable information about the extent to which the model exhibits behavior consistent with expectations from continuum quantum gravity, as well as revealing potential pathologies or unexpected features.

## A Surprising Discontinuity

Perhaps the most striking result of this investigation is the discovery of a discontinuity in the behavior of the model as the deformation parameter q approaches 1 through roots of unity. Naively, one might expect that as q tends toward 1—the value corresponding to the undeformed, classical limit of the quantum group structure—the q-deformed model should smoothly reduce to the original, non-deformed Barrett-Crane model. However, the numerical results reveal that this limit is not continuous: quantities computed for q at roots of unity approaching 1 do not converge to the corresponding quantities in the q=1 model. This unexpected discontinuity raises important questions about the interpretation of the q-deformed theory as a regularization or extension of the original model, and suggests that the relationship between the deformed and undeformed theories is considerably more subtle than previously assumed. This finding has significant implications for how the cosmological constant and the associated quantum group deformation should be understood within the broader framework of spin foam quantum gravity, and it motivates further analytical and numerical investigation into the nature of this limiting behavior.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these results demonstrate the power of numerical methods to uncover subtle and non-trivial features of spin foam models of quantum gravity that might not be readily apparent from formal analytical considerations alone. The extensions developed here—to q-deformed models and to arbitrary triangulations—provide a flexible toolkit for future numerical explorations of the Barrett-Crane model and related constructions, while the discovery of the discontinuity at roots of unity underscores the necessity of careful numerical scrutiny when studying the deformation parameters that appear throughout modern approaches to discretized quantum gravity.

# Numerical Investigation of q-Deformed Barrett-Crane Models in Riemannian Quantum Gravity

## Introduction

The Barrett-Crane model represents one of the most extensively studied approaches to quantum gravity within the spin foam formalism, providing a discrete, combinatorial framework for computing transition amplitudes between quantum states of geometry. Despite significant analytical progress in understanding the structure of these models, many essential questions regarding their physical behavior—particularly in the continuum or semiclassical limits—remain difficult to address through purely analytical means. This difficulty has motivated the development of numerical techniques capable of probing the model's behavior on finite triangulations, offering a complementary window into its deeper properties.

In this work, we extend previous numerical methods for studying Barrett-Crane models to encompass a broader class of scenarios, most notably the q-deformed version of the model, which is constructed using representations of the quantum group $SU(2)_q$ rather than the classical group $SU(2)$. The q-deformation is of particular interest because it is expected, via analogy with related models in three-dimensional gravity, to introduce an effective cosmological constant into the theory. Understanding how this deformation affects physical observables therefore offers valuable insight into how gravitational quantum dynamics might be modified in the presence of a nonzero cosmological constant.

## Methodology

Our numerical approach builds upon and generalizes existing computational frameworks that were previously restricted to specific triangulations and to the undeformed model. We have extended these techniques in two key directions:

**Arbitrary Triangulations:** Rather than restricting our attention to a small set of symmetric or simplified simplicial complexes, we develop tools capable of handling general triangulations of the underlying spacetime manifold. This generalization is crucial for probing whether observed behaviors are artifacts of high symmetry or genuine features of the model applicable across a wide range of discretizations.

**q-Deformation:** We incorporate the representation theory of quantum groups at roots of unity into our numerical framework, allowing us to compute spin foam amplitudes for the q-deformed Barrett-Crane model. This requires careful implementation of q-deformed 6j-symbols and related recoupling data, along with appropriate truncations of the state sum where necessary for computational tractability.

Using this extended framework, we compute expectation values of a range of physically motivated observables. Of particular interest is a **spin-spin correlation function**, which measures correlations between geometric quantities (associated with triangle areas, encoded by spin labels) at different locations within the triangulation. This observable serves as a probe of the correlation structure predicted by the quantum gravity path integral, offering a discretized analogue of correlation functions familiar from continuum quantum field theory and general relativity.

## Results

Our numerical investigations yield a striking and unexpected result: as the deformation parameter $q$ is taken to approach unity through a sequence of roots of unity (i.e., $q \to 1$ within the discrete set of values for which the quantum group representation theory is well-defined), the computed expectation values of our observables exhibit a **discontinuity**. Specifically, the limiting values obtained as $q \to 1$ along roots of unity do **not** coincide with the values computed directly in the undeformed ($q=1$, classical $SU(2)$) Barrett-Crane model.

This finding is surprising for several reasons:

1. **Naive Expectations:** One might expect that as the deformation parameter approaches the classical value, the q-deformed model should smoothly interpolate to the classical model, with the deformation acting as a small perturbation that vanishes in the limit. Our results indicate that this naive expectation fails.

2. **Cosmological Constant Analogy:** In related contexts, such as the Turaev-Viro model in three dimensions, the deformation parameter is understood to encode the cosmological constant, with the limit $q \to 1$ corresponding to the vanishing cosmological constant limit. Our discontinuity suggests that in four dimensions, within the Barrett-Crane framework, this naive dictionary between deformation and cosmological constant may not carry over straightforwardly, or that additional subtleties in the limiting procedure must be accounted for.

3. **Robustness Across Triangulations:** Notably, we find that this discontinuity persists across the range of triangulations we tested, suggesting that it is not simply a lattice artifact tied to a specific simplicial complex, but rather reflects a more fundamental structural feature of how the q-deformed and undeformed models relate to one another.

## Discussion and Implications

The discontinuity we observe raises important questions about the analytic structure of the Barrett-Crane model and its deformations. Several possible explanations and implications merit further investigation:

- **Non-uniform convergence:** It is possible that the limit $q \to 1$ is simply not uniform across the space of observables or triangulations, meaning that different subsequences of roots of unity, or different orders of limits (e.g., large triangulation limit versus $q \to 1$ limit), could yield different results. Untangling the order of limits may be essential to correctly interpreting the physical content of the q-deformed model.

- **Physical Interpretation of q-Deformation:** Our results suggest that the physical interpretation of the deformation parameter as directly analogous to a cosmological constant, smoothly connecting to the undeformed model at zero cosmological constant, may need to be reconsidered or refined in the four-dimensional Riemannian Barrett-Crane context.

- **Implications for Numerical Approaches to Spin Foam Models:** More broadly, this finding underscores the importance of numerical investigations as a tool for uncovering subtle and unexpected features of spin foam models that may not be readily apparent from formal or asymptotic analytic treatments alone.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates the power of extending numerical methods to explore previously inaccessible regimes of the Barrett-Crane model, including q-deformations and general triangulations. The discovery of a discontinuity in the $q \to 1$ limit through roots of unity represents a significant and unexpected result, one that challenges simple assumptions about the relationship between the q-deformed and classical models and opens new avenues for both numerical and analytical investigation into the structure of quantum gravity models based on spin foams. Future work will focus on elucidating the origin of this discontinuity, exploring its dependence on the choice of observables, and investigating its implications for the broader program of understanding the role of the cosmological constant within spin foam quantum gravity.

# The Barrett-Crane Model and Riemannian Quantum Gravity

The Barrett-Crane model represents one of the most significant contributions to the field of spin foam models in quantum gravity, developed by mathematical physicists John Barrett and Louis Crane in the late 1990s. This model emerged as an attempt to provide a rigorous, background-independent framework for quantizing gravity, building upon earlier work in loop quantum gravity and topological quantum field theory.

## Theoretical Foundations

At its core, the Barrett-Crane model discretizes four-dimensional spacetime using simplicial complexes—networks of triangulated building blocks (tetrahedra and 4-simplices) that approximate continuous geometry. The model assigns quantum states to these geometric structures using the representation theory of Lie groups, specifically SO(4) in the Riemannian signature case and the Lorentz group SO(3,1) in the physically relevant Lorentzian signature.

The Riemannian version of the model served as an important testing ground for the theory. Working with Riemannian geometry—where spacetime is treated with a positive-definite metric rather than the Lorentzian signature of physical spacetime—allowed Barrett and Crane to develop mathematical techniques in a somewhat simpler setting before tackling the more physically relevant but technically challenging Lorentzian case.

## The Simplicity Constraints

A key innovation of the Barrett-Crane construction was the introduction of "simplicity constraints." These constraints restrict the representations associated with the geometric data so that they correspond to genuine geometric tetrahedra rather than arbitrary algebraic structures. This was crucial for ensuring that the quantum states of the theory actually correspond to sensible classical geometries in an appropriate limit, addressing a fundamental challenge in translating abstract representation-theoretic data into physical geometric quantities.

## Significance and Legacy

The Barrett-Crane model was influential for several reasons:

- It provided one of the first well-defined spin foam models with a clear geometric interpretation
- It established connections between quantum gravity and topological quantum field theories, particularly through its relationship to the Ponzano-Regge model in three dimensions
- It stimulated significant mathematical development in the study of quantum groups and their representation theories
- It served as a precursor to later, more refined models such as the EPRL/FK model, which addressed some limitations of the original construction

While subsequent research revealed certain shortcomings in the Barrett-Crane model—particularly concerning the correct implementation of the simplicity constraints at the quantum level—it remains a foundational contribution to the spin foam approach to quantum gravity. The model's careful treatment of both Riemannian and Lorentzian signatures helped clarify the mathematical structures necessary for a consistent quantum theory of gravity, influencing the trajectory of research in this field for decades afterward.

# Spin Foam Models: Arbitrary Triangulations and Roots-of-Unity Deformation

## Overview

This research area addresses two significant challenges in loop quantum gravity's spin foam approach to quantum gravity: extending models beyond simple triangulations and incorporating quantum group deformations at roots of unity.

## Key Components

### 1. Arbitrary Triangulations
Traditional spin foam models (like the EPRL model) were originally formulated for specific simplicial structures. Extending to **arbitrary triangulations** involves:
- Generalizing vertex amplitudes beyond 4-simplex constraints
- Handling more complex combinatorial structures (irregular polytopes, non-simplicial cellular decompositions)
- Ensuring consistency conditions (like gluing/composition rules) hold across generic triangulations
- Addressing potential triangulation-dependence issues, which is crucial for demonstrating background independence

### 2. Roots-of-Unity Deformation
Using **quantum group parameters at roots of unity** (q = deformation parameter) rather than generic real values:
- Connects to Turaev-Viro/Chern-Simons theory with a **cosmological constant**
- The deformation parameter relates to Λ through q = exp(iπ/(k+2)) type relations
- Provides natural **finiteness** of state sums (unlike SU(2) models with infinite sums)
- Quantum group representation theory has finitely many irreducible representations, taming divergences

## Physical Motivations

- **Cosmological constant incorporation**: Root-of-unity models naturally encode Λ > 0 in the quantum gravity path integral
- **UV finiteness**: The quantum deformation regularizes sums over intermediate spins that would otherwise diverge
- **Semiclassical limit**: Recovering Regge calculus / general relativity with cosmological constant term in appropriate limits
- **Consistency with 3d results**: Building on Turaev-Viro model successes in 3d quantum gravity, extending insights to 4d

## Technical Challenges Addressed

1. **Vertex amplitude generalization**: Defining {6j}-symbol analogs for quantum groups on general graphs
2. **Gluing/composition consistency**: Ensuring amplitudes compose correctly when triangulations are refined or coarse-grained
3. **Asymptotic analysis**: Studying large-spin behavior to check for correct semiclassical (Regge) limit
4. **Reality conditions**: Managing the interplay between Lorentzian structure and root-of-unity (compact) quantum group representations

## Significance

This line of work aims to produce a **mathematically well-defined, finite spin foam model** that:
- Works on arbitrary discretizations (not just fixed triangulations), supporting genuine background independence
- Naturally includes a cosmological constant
- Provides a path toward defining the **continuum limit** via refinement of triangulations
- Connects loop quantum gravity approaches with categorical/TQFT methods

---

# Abstract

We present a numerical framework for computing spin-spin correlation functions in discretized quantum gravity models, with particular emphasis on lattice formulations coupled to matter fields exhibiting quenched disorder. Our approach combines transfer matrix methods with Monte Carlo sampling over fluctuating geometries, enabling efficient evaluation of two-point correlators $\langle S_i S_j \rangle$ across a range of deformation parameters $q$ that interpolate between classical and deeply quantum regimes of the underlying spin network. The algorithm employs an adaptive mesh refinement scheme near coincidence limits, together with importance sampling weighted by the Regge action, to control statistical noise in regions of large curvature fluctuation.

Applying this method to a family of quantum gravity models built on $q$-deformed spin networks, we compute correlation functions across simplicial complexes of varying topology and report their scaling behavior as functions of geodesic distance. While correlators vary smoothly for generic values of $q$, we find that in the limit $q \to 1$—corresponding to the recovery of the classical $SU(2)$ recoupling structure—the correlation function develops an unexpected discontinuity. This non-analytic behavior manifests as a jump in the long-distance decay exponent and a corresponding singularity in the associated susceptibility, signaling a qualitative reorganization of the underlying entanglement structure of the spin network states precisely at the classical limit.

We argue that this discontinuity is not a numerical artifact, having verified its persistence under lattice refinement, increased Monte Carlo statistics, and alternative discretization schemes for the deformed recoupling coefficients. Instead, we interpret it as evidence of a genuine phase-transition-like phenomenon separating quantum-deformed and classical regimes of the spin network, with possible implications for the semiclassical limit of loop quantum gravity and related discrete approaches to quantum spacetime. We discuss the sensitivity of this transition to boundary conditions and lattice topology, and outline directions for analytic understanding of the discontinuity via effective field theory arguments near $q=1$.

We present an extension of established numerical methods for spin foam models to the q-deformed Barrett-Crane model, which arises from the representation theory of the quantum group $SU_q(2)$ and is conjectured to encode a nonzero cosmological constant within the framework of loop quantum gravity. Building upon Monte Carlo integration techniques previously developed for the classical (undeformed) Barrett-Crane model, we adapt the computational framework to accommodate the modified amplitude structure, quantum dimensions, and fusion rules inherent to the q-deformed vertex and edge weights. The deformation parameter $q$, taken to be a root of unity, introduces a natural cutoff on the representation labels summed in the state-sum, rendering the model finite and computationally tractable for numerical evaluation at fixed and varying values of the deformation parameter.

We describe the algorithmic modifications required to implement the q-deformed 15j symbols and associated normalization factors, and we benchmark the resulting code against known analytic and semiclassical limits. Using this framework, we compute expectation values of geometric and curvature-related observables—including edge length operators and volume-type quantities—on triangulated simplicial complexes, and we examine their dependence on the deformation parameter and on the choice of boundary data. Our results are compared with corresponding computations in the undeformed model to assess the impact of the quantum group deformation on the statistical and geometric behavior of the state sum, including convergence properties, statistical fluctuations, and the approach to the semiclassical regime as $q \to 1$.

This work provides a practical computational toolkit for exploring q-deformed spin foam models numerically, offering a route toward quantitative investigation of the cosmological-constant-deformed sector of loop quantum gravity and establishing a foundation for future studies of dynamics, correlation functions, and continuum limits in quantum group spin foam models.

We investigate the behavior of Riemannian quantum gravity models constructed via quantum group deformations as the deformation parameter q approaches unity along a sequence of roots of unity. This limit is of particular interest because it connects the discrete, finite-dimensional structures characteristic of quantum group representation theory to the continuum limit expected to recover classical Riemannian geometry and standard quantum gravity behavior.

Furthermore, we identify a systematic pattern in the density and distribution of allowed representations near roots of unity, suggesting an underlying number-theoretic structure that governs the approach to the classical regime. These results support the interpretation of quantum-deformed Riemannian quantum gravity models as regularized, finite-dimensional approximations to continuum quantum gravity, with the root-of-unity limit providing a controlled pathway for extracting physical, cutoff-independent predictions.
